en: I would like coffee and water, please.
es: Quisiera café y agua, por favor.
note: Y joins items. Quisiera and por favor make a request more courteous.

en: I want to go, but I can't.
note: Pero introduces a contrast. Puedo is the yo form of poder.

en: I'm staying because it's raining.
note: Porque gives a reason; it is written as one word without an accent.

en: Although it's late, I'm going.
note: Aunque means although. Es states a fact here.

en: It's late, so I'm leaving.
es: Es tarde, así que me voy.
note: Así que introduces a result. Irse means to leave.

en: First we eat, then we go out.
note: Primero and luego put actions in order. Both verbs use nosotros forms.

en: Before leaving, I'll call you.
note: Antes de takes an infinitive. The present te llamo can express a planned action.

en: After eating, I rest.
note: Después de takes an infinitive: comer stays unconjugated.

en: Please come if you have time.
es: Por favor, ven si tienes tiempo.
note: Si + present expresses a realistic condition. Por favor softens the invitation.

en: Please let me know when you arrive.
note: Cuando + subjunctive llegues refers to a future arrival. Por favor makes the request polite.

en: While you cook, I clean.
note: Mientras connects simultaneous actions. Yo emphasizes who does the cleaning.

en: I also want to go.
note: También adds someone or something to the idea: also or too.

en: I don't know where it is.
note: Dónde means where in an indirect question: no sé dónde (I don't know where).

en: Where would you like to eat?
note: Dónde asks about a place. Te gustaría means you would like, a courteous way to ask a preference.

en: Besides, I need help.
note: Además adds another point. Necesito already identifies the speaker as I.

en: For example, we can go tomorrow.
note: Por ejemplo introduces an example. Podemos + infinitive means we can do something.

en: So, you're not coming?
note: O sea is a conversational way to clarify what someone means.

en: This is where I live.
note: Donde connects the place with what happens there. It has no accent in this relative clause.

en: Anyway, I'm going to try.
es: De todos modos, voy a intentarlo.
note: De todos modos means anyway. Voy a + infinitive expresses a plan.

en: That's why I called you.
note: Por eso points back to a reason. Llamé is completed past, I called.

en: Since you're here, please come in.
es: Ya que estás aquí, pasa, por favor.
note: Ya que introduces a reason. Pasa, por favor is a friendly, polite invitation.

en: Since it's closed, let's go somewhere else.
es: Como está cerrado, vamos a otro lugar.
note: Como at the start can mean since or because. Está cerrado describes its state.

en: Would you like tea or coffee?
note: O offers alternatives. Te gustaría makes a courteous offer to one person.

en: Please tell me where you're going.
note: Adónde asks about a destination. Por favor softens the informal command dime.

en: It's not today, but tomorrow.
note: Sino replaces a rejected alternative after a negative statement.

en: Then we can talk.
note: Entonces connects this idea to the previous one: then or in that case.

en: Despite the rain, we went out yesterday.
es: A pesar de la lluvia, salimos ayer.
note: A pesar de introduces an obstacle. Ayer makes clear that salimos refers to the past.

en: As soon as I arrive, I'll call you.
note: En cuanto + subjunctive llegue refers to a future arrival.

en: I'll stay here until you return.
es: Hasta que vuelvas, me quedo aquí.
note: Hasta que + subjunctive vuelvas describes a return that is still ahead.

en: Since I arrived, I've been feeling better.
note: Desde que marks a starting point. Llegué is past; estoy describes the current state.

en: Every time I go, I learn something.
es: Cada vez que voy, aprendo algo.
note: Cada vez que introduces a repeated event. Both verbs are present.

en: Whenever I can, I walk.
note: Siempre que + present describes a recurring situation here.

en: Just in case, please take some water.
es: Por si acaso, lleva agua, por favor.
note: Por si acaso means just in case. Por favor makes the suggestion courteous.

en: When do you finish work?
note: Cuándo has an accent in a question. Terminar de + infinitive means to finish doing something.

en: I'll wait where we met.
note: Donde introduces a place. Nos conocimos means we met each other.

en: I speak slowly so that you understand.
note: Para que expresses purpose and takes subjunctive entiendas.

en: I study in order to learn.
note: Para + infinitive expresses purpose when the same person performs both actions.

en: I'll go with you if you want.
note: Si can follow the main clause. Contigo means with you, for one informal listener.

en: When I was a boy, I lived here.
note: Era and vivía are imperfect forms describing a past stage of life.

en: In the end, everything went well.
note: Al final introduces the outcome. Salió is completed past, it turned out.

en: Meanwhile, please wait here.
es: Mientras tanto, espera aquí, por favor.
note: Mientras tanto means meanwhile. Por favor makes the instruction polite.

en: We'll talk about that later.
note: Después means later here. Present hablamos can express a future arrangement.

en: I used to work here before.
note: Antes means before or previously. Trabajaba describes a past habit.

en: Then, what do we do?
note: Entonces can introduce the next step or a conclusion.

en: Where are you from?
note: De dónde asks about origin. Eres is the tú form of ser.

en: In fact, I already knew that.
note: De hecho adds a fact. Sabía describes knowledge held in the past.

en: By the way, how are you?
note: Por cierto introduces a related comment or a change of topic.

en: Please let me know when you're ready.
es: Por favor, avísame cuando estés listo.
note: Cuando + subjunctive estés refers to a future state. Use lista when addressing a woman. Por favor is polite.

en: That is, we have to wait.
note: Es decir clarifies an idea. Tener que + infinitive expresses necessity.

en: I don't know when he's coming.
note: Cuándo keeps its accent in an indirect question. Viene is the él/ella/usted form of venir.
